children: President Donald Trump said Sunday that his administration plans to announce additional investments in U.S. manufacturing, following Volkswagen's
disclosure of plans to build an Audi factory in Georgia, as Republicans seek to strengthen their economic message ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

, Trump said his administration has “many other announcements” forthcoming as he campaigns for Republican candidates. The president also highlighted the need for additional workers to support industrial expansion, saying, “The biggest thing we need are construction workers.”

Audi plant and the prospect of additional manufacturing projects could signal opportunities for construction companies, industrial equipment suppliers and businesses tied to automotive production. However, the economic benefits will depend on the size and timing of the investments, labor availability and whether higher borrowing and construction costs affect companies' expansion plans.

Audi's proposed Georgia facility represents a $4.2 billion investment that could create approximately 4,500 jobs and eventually produce 200,000 SUVs annually, the Associated Press reported. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2027, with production expected in the early 2030s. However, Volkswagen's supervisory board must still give final approval for the project.
Trump has credited his tariffs on imported automobiles and other products with encouraging foreign manufacturers to expand U.S. production. Volkswagen

has faced substantial tariff costs because Audi currently imports all its vehicles sold in the American market from Europe and Mexico. Critics argue that the tariffs have also increased vehicle prices and discouraged some investments.

The manufacturing announcement comes as Republicans face mounting political pressure over inflation and gasoline prices. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released last week found that Trump's approval rating had fallen to 31%, while 68% of respondents disapproved of his handling of the economy. Democrats led Republicans by 47% to 35% among registered voters asked which party they would support in congressional elections.

Affordability has emerged as a central issue in the campaign. A Pew Research Center survey found that 84% of registered voters consider the economy very important to their midterm vote. Meanwhile, an Associated Press-NORC poll found that only 17% of Americans approved of Trump's handling of the cost of living, while 65% blamed his policies for persistently high prices.

Gasoline prices have become a particularly sensitive issue. An NBC News survey found that 67% of Americans considered gasoline costs a serious problem, while September's annual inflation rate reached 3.7%, driven partly by higher energy prices.

The election will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress for the final two years of Trump's presidency. Although new factory investments could bolster the administration's argument that its trade policies are revitalizing American manufacturing, the projects' longer-term economic benefits may do little to alleviate the immediate financial pressures facing voters.
